dos0: The DOST Break: A 5-Minute Self-Compassion Exercise | İhsan Eren
dos1: Four steps to treat yourself like a friend on a hard day: stop and name it, drop your shoulders, speak kindly, say thank you. A guided five-minute break.
dos2: The DOST break: five minutes of being a friend to yourself
dos3: If your closest friend were having a hard day, what would you say to them? Most likely something far gentler than what you say to yourself on the same kind of day. The DOST break turns that voice towards you for five minutes. “Dost” is Turkish for a true friend, and its letters name the four steps: Dur (stop), Omuzlarını bırak (drop your shoulders), Seslen (speak to yourself), Teşekkür et (say thank you). By the end you will have written yourself a short note.
dos5: Total time for the four steps; all you need is a quiet corner
dos7: How long the soothing touch lasted in a study where it lowered the stress-hormone response
dos9: How long people wrote to themselves as a friend would; the lift in mood was followed for months
dos11: A review of randomised controlled trials testing self-compassion practices
dos13: Silence your phone and sit somewhere comfortable. There is no rush; stay with each step for as long as you like.
dos19: Pause for a moment. Which of these is most present in you right now? There is no right or wrong answer; pick the one that feels closest.
dos31: Let your shoulders drop away from your ears and unclench your jaw. Place one hand over your heart and the other on your belly, and feel the warmth of your hands. Tap Start, then simply stay like this for 20 seconds.
dos33: If your closest friend were in your place today, what would you say to them? Now speak to yourself in that same voice. Add your name if you like, then choose the sentence that does you the most good.
dos36: The sentence you will say to yourself
dos37: You’re having a hard day; I can see that.
dos38: You’re doing the best you can. For today, that is enough.
dos39: Feeling this way is deeply human. You are not alone.
dos40: You have every right to slow down.
dos41: Making a mistake has not made you worth any less.
dos43: For the last step, turn to your body. Look not at how it appears but at what it did for you today, and thank it in one sentence.
dos44: A sentence of thanks to your body
dos45: You got me on my feet again today.
dos46: You carried me in spite of the pain.
dos47: You let me hug someone I love.
dos48: You told me you were tired; I heard you.
dos49: You breathed thousands of times without my noticing.
dos51: You wrote this to yourself. Read it slowly, in your own head.
dos53: What you write stays on this device, only while this page is open; it is not sent or saved anywhere.
dos55: So, {x}. You have named it; now let’s make a little room for it.
dos56: Not being able to name it is an answer too. Now let’s make a little room for it.
dos57: Feel the warmth of your hands
dos58: Let your breath flow at its own pace
dos59: Good. Carry on whenever you’re ready.
dos62: Today you feel {x}. I noticed, and I’m not brushing it aside.
dos63: Today there is something in you that you can’t name. That’s all right; noticing it is enough.
dos64: I have something to say to my body too: {x} Thank you.
dos68: You don’t have to do the four steps in order. Even the 20-second touch is a break in its own right.
dos70: Each step rests on a small practice that has been studied on its own. We have written what was found, along with what was not.
dos71: When you are inside a feeling, everything blurs together. Giving it a name puts a little distance between you and it. In a brain-imaging study, when 30 people chose a word for the emotion while looking at angry and frightened faces, the brain’s alarm centre (the amygdala) was less active.
dos72: Touch is the body’s oldest language of comfort. In a study of 159 people put through a stressful test, those who placed their hands on their heart and belly for 20 seconds had lower levels of the stress hormone cortisol than those who did not. Heart rate and how stressed they felt did not differ.
dos73: When we talk to ourselves, we are often our own harshest critic. Across seven studies with 585 people in total, those who addressed themselves by name rather than as “I” felt less distress in stressful situations. And people who wrote to themselves as a friend would for seven days were less depressed three months later and happier six months later.
dos74: We tend to notice our body only when it hurts or in the mirror. In a study of 81 young women who were unhappy with their bodies, those who wrote about what their body can do became more satisfied with it, and the effect was still there a week later.
dos76: The DOST break is not a treatment; it is five minutes you set aside for yourself. Each of the four steps has been studied separately, but combined in this order they have not been tested as a whole. The sequence was put together for this site.
dos77: In a review of 27 randomised controlled trials testing self-compassion practices, stress, depression and anxiety improved to a moderate degree. The authors also note that the trials differed widely from one another and that positive results may have been more likely to be published.
dos79: On an evening when the pain is worse and you are about to get angry with your body.
dos80: On a day you skipped your exercises and have started blaming yourself.
dos81: Straight after hard news or a hurtful conversation.
dos82: Before sleep, as you close the day.
dos83: If you’d like to calm the body first, see The 5-minute cyclic sighing breath; if you’d like to reach out to someone else, see Social connection and health.
dos85: No. Self-pity says “why always me” and leaves you isolated. Self-compassion says “this is hard, and I’m not the only one who struggles”. The aim is not to fool yourself or dodge responsibility; it is to be as fair to yourself as you would be to a friend you love.
dos86: Putting my hand on my heart feels odd. What should I do?
dos87: That’s perfectly natural. In the study, participants chose the touch that suited them; nearly all placed one hand on the heart and the other on the belly. You could cross your arms and hold your shoulders, or rest one hand inside the other. It can be done without anyone noticing, even on the bus.
dos88: How often should I do it?
dos89: There’s no rule. In the letter study, participants wrote on seven days in a row; you could try it for a week and see how you feel. A single round straight after a hard moment is fine too.
dos90: What if I feel worse while doing it?
dos91: When you start being gentle with yourself, feelings you have put off for a long time may come to the surface. Shorten the break, do only the touch step, or pause. If the distress continues, don’t carry it alone; talk to a mental health professional.
dos92: Getting support matters: If low mood, anxiety or sleep problems that have lasted for weeks are not easing with practices like these, see a doctor or a mental health professional. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call 112.
